simd.name: SIMD
simd.definition: Single instruction, multiple data: one instruction applies an operation across several lanes.
simd.explanation: A 256-bit AVX register can hold eight f32 values, while a 512-bit AVX-512 register can hold sixteen. Vector kernels load complete groups, compute lane-wise, and often reduce lanes to a scalar. SIMD can increase arithmetic throughput, but memory traffic, reduction overhead, dependencies, and CPU frequency can limit gains. The same executable must retain a safe fallback for architectures or CPUs without the requested instruction set.

scalar-tail.name: Scalar tail
scalar-tail.definition: Elements left after processing every complete SIMD-width group.
scalar-tail.explanation: For length N and lane width W, the tail has N modulo W values. A safe vector loop runs only while at least W elements remain, then ordinary scalar code processes the suffix. This handles empty, short, odd, and exact-multiple lengths without padding or out-of-bounds loads. Masked vector operations are another option on some architectures, but a scalar tail is portable, easy to verify, and sufficient until measurement proves tail cost matters.

auto-vectorization.name: Auto-vectorization
auto-vectorization.definition: A compiler transformation from scalar source operations to vector instructions.
auto-vectorization.explanation: LLVM’s vectorizers analyze loop legality, dependencies, aliases, target capabilities, and estimated cost. Independent elementwise loops are often easier to transform than floating-point reductions whose reassociation changes rounding. Optimized compilation enables the machinery, but source code has no universal promise that a specific loop vectorizes. Inspect generated code or optimization remarks before making that claim, and benchmark the resulting function with correctness checks and observable outputs.

runtime-feature-dispatch.name: Runtime feature dispatch
runtime-feature-dispatch.definition: Selecting an implementation after detecting instruction support on the CPU currently running the program.
runtime-feature-dispatch.explanation: A portable x86 binary can contain scalar and target-feature functions. The generic caller uses is_x86_feature_detected! and invokes an AVX function only when every required capability is present. Architecture cfg gates keep x86 intrinsics out of other targets. The target-feature call is unsafe because executing unsupported instructions is undefined behavior; runtime checks, equal lengths, and proven in-bounds loads form the documented safety argument.

checks: Portable lane sums match worked values and f64 over empty/short/odd lengths
Forced scalar and default dispatch match f64; AVX2+FMA and AVX-512F execute only when supported
Last-element impulses catch dropped tails; invalid shapes/nonfinite inputs/overflow rejected
Dense integration retains W[n,k], bias once, and varied-shape oracle agreement
limitations: Explicit SIMD implementations cover x86/x86_64 but not ARM NEON
The project uses scalar tails rather than masked AVX-512 loads
Default selection prefers AVX2/FMA and does not auto-tune backends
Auto-vectorization must be inspected for each compiler and target
No speedup is claimed without local release measurements
